headline: reMarkable Paper Pure: Distraction-free writing tablet reviewed
summary: The $399 reMarkable Paper Pure tablet aims to offer a focused writing and reading experience, free from digital distractions.
details: The new reMarkable Paper Pure, priced at $399, is the latest offering from the company focused on emulating the pen-and-paper writing experience. It's designed for writers, designers, and researchers who seek a distraction-free digital environment, eschewing notifications and multitasking apps.

This monochrome tablet features a 10.3-inch display, similar in size to its predecessor, the reMarkable 2. However, it boasts a flipped resolution for a wider and shorter screen, allowing more text to fit horizontally, enhancing both reading and writing comfort.

Beyond hardware refinements, the Paper Pure introduces enhanced software features. Users can now sync their calendars to access meeting details directly on the device and begin taking notes within specific meeting blocks, streamlining workflow.
Handwritten notes can be converted and shared with a single tap, generating an email link for easy distribution. The device also offers improved note searching capabilities across all your jottings.

For external content, users can send articles directly to the tablet as native notebooks, allowing for highlighting and annotation before sending them to the web app. Integration with cloud services like Drive, Dropbox, and OneDrive is also improved for importing and exporting documents.

While the Paper Pure excels at its core promise of distraction-free note-taking and sketching, its PDF handling remains suboptimal, and the e-reading experience doesn't rival dedicated e-readers like Kindle. It's positioned as a specialized work device rather than an all-in-one gadget.

Despite its premium price point, the reMarkable Paper Pure delivers on its core promise of a focused writing environment. The device encourages users to disconnect from the usual digital distractions, making it a compelling tool for drafting ideas and rough drafts.

headline_marked: Florida Man Arrested for [[$220K Crypto Theft]] via Malware in Steam Games
headline: Florida Man Arrested for $220K Crypto Theft via Malware in Steam Games
summary: An alleged operator of a malware scheme embedded in video games has been arrested, with authorities linking him to the theft of over $220,000 from approximately 8,000 infected devices.
details: Federal agents have arrested 21-year-old Zyaire Dontaevious Zamarion Wilkins in Florida, charging him with conspiracy to obtain information for financial gain. The FBI alleges Wilkins was involved in an operation that used malware hidden in eight video games distributed through a popular digital storefront, infecting around 8,000 devices.

The scheme, which ran from May 2024 to February 2026, allegedly stole at least $220,000 from roughly 80 cryptocurrency wallets. Investigators traced stolen Bitcoin to over 150 gift cards, many of which were used for food delivery services.

Wilkins is accused of financing and marketing the malware, rather than developing it. He reportedly operated under the handle Sibel.eth and was linked to a $10,000 purchase of a remote access trojan. The complaint mentions a search of the unidentified developer's home, where Signal chats tied Wilkins to discussions about tricking victims into approving transactions that drained their wallets.

The conspirators promoted the infected games on platforms like Discord, Telegram, X, and LinkedIn, using bots to target users with large cryptocurrency holdings. This targeted approach resulted in an approximate 1% hit rate, draining about 80 wallets from the 8,000 infected devices.

One of the games, BlockBlasters, is estimated by blockchain investigators to have stolen over $150,000 from hundreds of victims. This included $32,000 in cancer treatment funds stolen from a Twitch streamer in September 2025.

Payments from the operation's Bitcoin wallet were converted into gift cards via Bitrefill, with authorities linking these purchases to an Uber Eats account used at Wilkins' family home and university addresses. A search of his residence uncovered several devices and cryptocurrency wallet seed phrases.

Wilkins faces up to 10 years in prison if convicted. This arrest marks the first publicly reported action in the ongoing investigation into malware distributed through the Steam storefront, which has seen multiple similar incidents.
Valve, the parent company of Steam, has not yet responded to requests for comment regarding the incident. The investigation is being prosecuted in Seattle federal court, near Valve's headquarters.
